The early life stages of Dromus dromas are characterized by a brief embryonic phase, with fertilized ova hatching and the resulting veliger larvae beginning exogenous feeding after just 10 days [ab = 10 days] when water temperatures are held at a stable 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. Upon hatching, the shell length of the newly emerged veliger is a mere 0.02 centimeters [Lb = 0.02 centimeters], reflecting the minute size of the yolk-dependent, lecithotrophic larva at the moment of egg capsule rupture. Following a short planktonic period, these larvae attain a settlement-competent stage characterized by a shell length of approximately 0.03 centimeters , at which point they actively seek a suitable substrate for attachment and metamorphosis. This larval-juvenile transition involves a profound morphological transformation, including the loss of the velum and the development of functional gills, marking the onset of benthic life.

After metamorphosis and settlement, the post-larval juveniles of Dromus dromas begin a protracted phase of somatic growth that eventually culminates in the attainment of an ultimate shell length of 7.5 centimeters [Li = 7.5 centimeters]. This asymptotic size is reached only after several years of continuous shell accretion, a pattern consistent with the relatively slow growth rates observed in many freshwater unionid mussels. The maximum adult body mass corresponding to this length has been estimated at 15.1 grams [Wwi = 15.1 grams], a value derived from a size-corrected allometric relationship established for the related species Unio tumidus. This modest wet weight, combined with the elongated shell morphology, suggests a conservative energetic strategy whereby metabolic resources are channeled preferentially into structural growth rather than rapid tissue accumulation. Field surveys indicate that individuals approaching this ultimate size are typically several decades old, having survived the considerable predation and environmental stochasticity characteristic of their lotic habitats.

Sexual maturation in Dromus dromas is directly correlated with shell size rather than chronological age, and field data indicate that individuals first attain reproductive maturity at a shell length of 3 centimeters [Lp = 3 centimeters]. At this size, gonadal activity commences and gametogenesis proceeds, enabling the onset of breeding during the subsequent reproductive season. The initiation of spawning in this species has been observed to occur at an age of ten days [ab = ten days] after hatching under controlled conditions maintained at 14 °C [T = 14 °C], though this surprisingly rapid onset of reproductive capacity in the laboratory may reflect an artifact of the constant, optimal thermal regime rather than a reliable estimate for wild populations. In natural environments, the timing of first reproduction is likely delayed by slower somatic growth under variable temperature and food availability. Nonetheless, the ability to become reproductively active at such a small body size is an unusual trait among freshwater unionids.

The lifespan of Dromus dromas is remarkably extended, with the oldest documented individuals reaching an age of 25 years [am = 25 years] when maintained under stable environmental conditions at a temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. This longevity, equivalent to approximately 9125 days, places the species among the longer-lived members of the Unionidae, a family renowned for its slow life-history pace. Such an extended lifespan is consistent with a life-history strategy that delays senescence in favor of multiple reproductive episodes spread over many decades. In comparison, related species such as Unio tumidus exhibit maximal longevities of similar magnitude, though the specific value of 25 years [am = 25 years] recorded for Dromus dromas may represent an upper limit attainable only under the relatively benign conditions of a controlled laboratory setting, where predation and habitat disturbance are minimized at a temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C].

The post-settlement growth trajectory of Dromus dromas is well described by a decelerating curve, with the earliest benthic juveniles measuring just 0.03 centimeters  in shell length at the moment of metamorphic climax, a value that underscores the extreme vulnerability of this species to predation and physical displacement during the initial months of benthic life. Over the succeeding years, these spat gradually approach the ultimate shell length of 7.5 centimeters [Li = 7.5 centimeters], though growth rates slow considerably as individuals near this asymptote. The maximum recorded longevity of 25 years [am = 25 years] in this species aligns with the slow maturation and low annual metabolic expenditure typical of filter-feeding bivalves inhabiting temperate rivers, where seasonal resource pulses and low water temperatures impose a conservative energetic regime at a temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. This interplay between small initial size, protracted growth, and remarkable longevity provides a valuable model for understanding the demographic responses of freshwater mussels to environmental change.
